AlgebraicGeometry.RingedSpace.basicOpen.fullDefinition: def basicOpen {U : Opens X} (f : X.presheaf.obj (op U)) : Opens X where   -- Porting note: `coe` does not work   carrier := Subtype.val '' { x : U | IsUnit (X.presheaf.germ x f) }   is_open' := by     rw [isOpen_iff_forall_mem_open]     rintro _ ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩     obtain ⟨V, i, hxV, hf⟩ := X.isUnit_res_of_isUnit_germ U f x hx     use V.1     refine ⟨?_, V.2, hxV⟩     intro y hy     use (⟨y, i.le hy⟩ : U)     rw [Set.mem_setOf_eq]     constructor     · convert RingHom.isUnit_map (X.presheaf.germ ⟨y, hy⟩) hf       exact (X.presheaf.germ_res_apply i ⟨y, hy⟩ f).symm     · rfl set_option linter.uppercaseLean3 false in

  (f : X.toSheafedSpace ≅ Y.toSheafedSpace) : X ≅ Y
AlgebraicGeometry.LocallyRingedSpace.iso.comment:
Given two locally ringed spaces `X` and `Y`, an isomorphism between `X` and `Y` as _sheafed_
spaces can be lifted to an isomorphism `X ⟶ Y` as locally ringed spaces.

This is related to the property that the functor `forget_to_SheafedSpace` reflects isomorphisms.
In fact, it is slightly stronger as we do not require `f` to come from a morphism between
_locally_ ringed spaces.

AlgebraicGeometry.LocallyRingedSpace.Has.fullDefinition: instance coequalizer_π_stalk_isLocalRingHom (x : Y) :     IsLocalRingHom (PresheafedSpace.stalkMap (coequalizer.π f.val g.val : _) x) := by   constructor   rintro a ha   rcases TopCat.Presheaf.germ_exist _ _ a with ⟨U, hU, s, rfl⟩   erw [PresheafedSpace.stalkMap_germ_apply (coequalizer.π f.1 g.1 : _) U ⟨_, hU⟩] at ha   let V := imageBasicOpen f g U s   have hV : (coequalizer.π f.1 g.1).base ⁻¹' ((coequalizer.π f.1 g.1).base '' V.1) = V.1 :=     imageBasicOpen_image_preimage f g U s   have hV' :     V = ⟨(coequalizer.π f.1 g.1).base ⁻¹' ((coequalizer.π f.1 g.1).base '' V.1), hV.symm ▸ V.2⟩ :=     SetLike.ext' hV.symm   have V_open : IsOpen ((coequalizer.π f.val g.val).base '' V.1) :=     imageBasicOpen_image_open f g U s   have VleU : (⟨(coequalizer.π f.val g.val).base '' V.1, V_open⟩ : TopologicalSpace.Opens _) ≤ U :=     Set.image_subset_iff.mpr (Y.toRingedSpace.basicOpen_le _)   have hxV : x ∈ V := ⟨⟨_, hU⟩, ha, rfl⟩   erw [←     (coequalizer f.val g.val).presheaf.germ_res_apply (homOfLE VleU)       ⟨_, @Set.mem_image_of_mem _ _ (coequalizer.π f.val g.val).base x V.1 hxV⟩ s]   apply RingHom.isUnit_map   rw [← isUnit_map_iff ((coequalizer.π f.val g.val : _).c.app _), ← comp_apply,     NatTrans.naturality, comp_apply, ← isUnit_map_iff (Y.presheaf.map (eqToHom hV').op)]   -- Porting note (#11224): change `rw` to `erw`   erw [← comp_apply, ← comp_apply, ← Y.presheaf.map_comp]   convert @RingedSpace.isUnit_res_basicOpen Y.toRingedSpace (unop _)       (((coequalizer.π f.val g.val).c.app (op U)) s)

explanatories.AlgebraicGeometry.PresheafedSpace.IsOpen: This theorem establishes that if a morphism between presheafed spaces is an open immersion, then the underlying sheaf morphism is an isomorphism for every open subset of the source space.

pullback.fst _ _   c :=     { app := fun U =>         hf.invApp (unop U) ≫           g.c.app (op (hf.base_open.isOpenMap.functor.obj (unop U))) ≫             Y.presheaf.map               (eqToHom                 (by                   simp only [IsOpenMap.functor, Subtype.mk_eq_mk, unop_op, op_inj_iff, Opens.map,                     Subtype.coe_mk, Functor.op_obj]                   apply LE.le.antisymm                   · rintro _ ⟨_, h₁, h₂⟩                     use (TopCat.pullbackIsoProdSubtype _ _).inv ⟨⟨_, _⟩, h₂⟩                     -- Porting note: need a slight hand holding                     -- used to be `simpa using h₁` before #13170                     change _ ∈ _ ⁻¹' _ ∧ _                     simp only [TopCat.coe_of, restrict_carrier, Set.preimage_id', Set.mem_preimage,                       SetLike.mem_coe]                     constructor                     · change _ ∈ U.unop at h₁                       convert h₁                       erw [TopCat.pullbackIsoProdSubtype_inv_fst_apply]                     · erw [TopCat.pullbackIsoProdSubtype_inv_snd_apply]                   · rintro _ ⟨x, h₁, rfl⟩                     -- next line used to be                     --  `exact ⟨_, h₁, ConcreteCategory.congr_hom pullback.condition x⟩))`                     -- before #13170                     refine ⟨_, h₁, ?_⟩                     change (_ ≫ f.base) _ = (_ ≫ g.base) _                     rw [pullback.condition]))       naturality := by         intro U V i         induction U using Opposite.rec'         induction V using Opposite.rec' AlgebraicGeometry.PresheafedSpace.IsOpen.comment:
The universal property of open immersions:
For an open immersion `f : X ⟶ Z`, given any morphism of schemes `g : Y ⟶ Z` whose topological
image is contained in the image of `f`, we can lift this morphism to a unique `Y ⟶ X` that
commutes with these maps.

  [PreservesLimits (CategoryTheory.forget C)] [PreservesFilteredColimits (CategoryTheory.forget C)]

AlgebraicGeometry.SheafedSpace.IsOpenImm.comment:

whose forgetful functor reflects isomorphisms, preserves limits and filtered colimits.

is an open immersion iff every stalk map is an iso.

AlgebraicGeometry.SheafedSpace.IsOpenImm.fullDefinition: instance sigma_ι_isOpenImmersion [HasStrictTerminalObjects C] :     SheafedSpace.IsOpenImmersion (colimit.ι F i) where   base_open := sigma_ι_openEmbedding F i   c_iso U := by     have e : colimit.ι F i = _ :=       (ι_preservesColimitsIso_inv SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace F i).symm     have H :       OpenEmbedding         (colimit.ι (F ⋙ SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace) i ≫             (preservesColimitIso SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace F).inv).base :=       e ▸ sigma_ι_openEmbedding F i     suffices IsIso <| (colimit.ι (F ⋙ SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace) i ≫         (preservesColimitIso SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace F).inv).c.app <|       op (H.isOpenMap.functor.obj U) by       -- Porting note (#11083): just `convert` is very slow, so helps it a bit       convert this using 2 <;> congr     rw [PresheafedSpace.comp_c_app,       ← PresheafedSpace.colimitPresheafObjIsoComponentwiseLimit_hom_π]     -- Porting note: this instance created manually to make the `inferInstance` below work     have inst1 : IsIso (preservesColimitIso forgetToPresheafedSpace F).inv.c :=       PresheafedSpace.c_isIso_of_iso _     rsuffices : IsIso         (limit.π           (PresheafedSpace.componentwiseDiagram (F ⋙ SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace)             ((Opens.map                   (preservesColimitIso SheafedSpace.forgetToPresheafedSpace F).inv.base).obj               (unop <| op <| H.isOpenMap.functor.obj U)))           (op i))     · infer_instance     apply limit_π_isIso_of_is_strict_terminal     intro j hj     induction j using Opposite.rec' with | h j => ?_     dsimp     convert (F.obj j).sheaf.isTerminalOfEmpty using 3     convert image_preimage_is_empty F i j (fun h => hj (congr_arg op h.symm)) U using 6     exact (congr_arg PresheafedSpace.Hom.base e).symm

AlgebraicGeometry.LocallyRingedSpace.IsO.comment:
The universal property of open immersions:
For an open immersion `f : X ⟶ Z`, given any morphism of schemes `g : Y ⟶ Z` whose topological
image is contained in the image of `f`, we can lift this morphism to a unique `Y ⟶ X` that
commutes with these maps.

EuclideanGeometry.mul_dist_le_mul_dist_a.comment:

explanatories.RingHom.id: This definition describes the identity ring homomorphism that maps each element of a semiring to itself.
explanatories.LinearMap.isometryOfInner: This definition establishes that a linear map that preserves the inner product between two inner product spaces is classified as a linear isometry.
explanatories.Real.Angle.cos: The definition specifies that the cosine function is applied to an angle, resulting in a real number value.
explanatories.LinearMap.id: This definition specifies the identity linear map for a module over a semiring that maps each element to itself.
explanatories.Real.Angle.sin: The definition specifies the sine function as it applies to angles in the real number system.
explanatories.LinearIsometryEquiv.toLinearEquiv: This definition establishes that a linear isometry equivalence between two seminormed modules can be interpreted as a linear equivalence while preserving the underlying structure.
explanatories.RCLike.conj_to_real: This theorem states that the conjugate of a real number is equal to the number itself.
explanatories.id: The identity function returns its input unchanged and can be used to explicitly assign a type to an expression for typeclass inference purposes.
explanatories.LinearMap.smul_apply: This theorem states that applying a scalar multiplication to a linear map and then to a vector results in the same output as applying the scalar multiplication directly to the image of the vector under the linear map.
explanatories.LinearMap.add_apply: This theorem states that the sum of two linear maps applied to an element of their domain equals the sum of the results obtained by applying each individual map to that element.
explanatories.LinearMap.id_coe: This theorem shows that the identity linear map is equivalent to the usual identity function when viewed as a function from a module over a semiring.
explanatories.LinearEquiv.coe_coe: This theorem states that the function obtained by coercing a linear equivalence to a linear map is equal to the function directly associated with that linear equivalence.
explanatories.LinearIsometryEquiv.coe_toLinearEquiv: This theorem states that the function associated with a linear isometry equivalence is equal to the function corresponding to its underlying linear equivalence.
explanatories.Orientation.areaForm_rightAngleRotation_: This theorem states that in a two-dimensional oriented inner product space, the area form evaluated at a vector rotated by a right angle will equal the negative inner product of that vector with another given vector.
explanatories.Orientation.inner_rightAngleRotation_lef: This theorem shows that the inner product of a vector with another vector after applying a right-angle rotation in a two-dimensional oriented inner product space is equal to the area form of the first vector with respect to the second vector.
explanatories.Orientation.inner_rightAngleRotation_rig: This theorem states that the inner product of a vector with the result of a right angle rotation applied to another vector in a two-dimensional oriented inner product space is equal to the negative of the area form applied to the first vector and the second vector.
explanatories.inner_add_left: This theorem asserts that the inner product of the sum of two vectors with a third vector is equal to the sum of the inner products of each vector with the third vector.
explanatories.inner_smul_left: This theorem establishes that the inner product of a scalar multiple of a vector with another vector equals the scalar (understood as its conjugate) multiplied by the inner product of the original vector with the other vector.
explanatories.inner_add_right: This theorem states that the inner product of a vector with the sum of two other vectors is equal to the sum of the inner products of the first vector with each of the two vectors being added.
explanatories.inner_smul_right: This theorem states that the inner product of a vector with a scalar multiple of another vector is equal to the scalar multiplied by the inner product of the original vectors.
explanatories.Inner.inner: The inner product function represents a mapping from pairs of elements in a vector space to a scalar field.
explanatories.Real.Angle.cos_sq_add_sin_sq: The theorem establishes that the sum of the square of the cosine and the square of the sine of an angle is equal to one.
explanatories.Exists.intro: If there is an element that satisfies a property, then it can be used to demonstrate the existence of at least one such element with that property.
explanatories.And.intro: This states that if two propositions are true, then their conjunction is also true.
explanatories.Iff.intro: Two propositions are equivalent if one implies the other in both directions.

Affine.Triangle.circumsphere_eq_of_dist_.code:
Affine.Triangle.circumsphere_eq_of_dist_of_oangle.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup V]

  Simplex.circumsphere t =
    {
      center :=
        ((∡ (t.points i₁) (t.points i₂) (t.points i₃)).tan⁻¹ / 2) •
            (o.rotation ↑(π / 2)) (t.points i₃ -ᵥ t.points i₁) +ᵥ
          midpoint ℝ (t.points i₁) (t.points i₃),
      radius := dist (t.points i₁) (t.points i₃) / |(∡ (t.points i₁) (t.points i₂) (t.points i₃)).sin| / 2 }

The circumsphere of a triangle may be expressed explicitly in terms of two points and the
angle at the third point.

explanatories.AffineSubspace.comap: This definition describes the preimage of an affine subspace under an affine map, which is itself an affine subspace.
explanatories.AffineEquiv.vaddConst: This definition specifies an affine equivalence between a vector space and an affine space by associating each vector with the result of adding a fixed point in the affine space.
explanatories.AffineEquiv.symm: This definition describes the process of obtaining the inverse of an affine equivalence, resulting in another affine equivalence between the two original affine spaces in reverse order.
explanatories.LinearMap.ker: The kernel of a linear map is defined as the set of elements in the domain that are mapped to zero in the codomain, and it forms a submodule of the domain.
explanatories.Submodule.toAffineSubspace: This definition establishes a method to treat a submodule of a vector space as an affine subspace.
explanatories.Iff.symm: If two propositions are equivalent, then their equivalence can be reversed.

AffineSubspace.perpBisector.fullDefinition: def perpBisector (p₁ p₂ : P) : AffineSubspace ℝ P :=   .comap ((AffineEquiv.vaddConst ℝ (midpoint ℝ p₁ p₂)).symm : P →ᵃ[ℝ] V) <|     (LinearMap.ker (innerₛₗ ℝ (p₂ -ᵥ p₁))).toAffineSubspace
AffineSubspace.perpBisector.description: This definition describes the perpendicular bisector of a segment in a Euclidean affine space as a specific type of affine subspace.

explanatories.vadd_vsub_assoc: This theorem asserts that in an additive torsor, adding a group element to one point and then subtracting another point yields the same result as first subtracting the two points and then adding the group element.
explanatories.add_sub_assoc: In a subtracted negative monoid, the sum of an element and another element minus a third element equals the sum of the first element and the difference of the second element and the third element.
explanatories.AffineSubspace.direction: This definition describes the direction of an affine subspace as the submodule formed by the differences of pairs of points within that subspace, with the exception of the zero submodule for an empty affine subspace.
explanatories.Eq.symm: Equality is symmetric, meaning that if one element is equal to another, then the second is equal to the first.
explanatories.Ne.symm: If two elements are not equal to each other, then reversing their order also indicates that they are not equal.
explanatories.Exists.intro: If there is an element that satisfies a property, then it can be used to demonstrate the existence of at least one such element with that property.
explanatories.AffineSubspace.direction_mk': This theorem establishes that the direction of an affine subspace created from a given point and its associated directional submodule is equal to that submodule.
explanatories.EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjectionFn: The orthogonal projection of a point onto a nonempty affine subspace is defined as a function that produces the point's closest position within that subspace.
explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

explanatories.EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjectionFn: The orthogonal projection of a point onto a given affine subspace is guaranteed to lie within that subspace.
explanatories.AffineSubspace.self_mem_mk': This theorem asserts that a point included in the definition of an affine subspace will always belong to that subspace when it is formed from the point and a specified direction.
explanatories.EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjectionFn: The difference between a point and its orthogonal projection onto a subspace lies in the direction orthogonal to that subspace.
explanatories.AffineSubspace.vadd_mem_of_mem_direction: This theorem asserts that adding a vector from the direction of an affine subspace to any point within that subspace results in another point that remains within the same subspace.
explanatories.AffineSubspace.vsub_right_mem_direction_: This theorem asserts that the difference between a point in an affine subspace and another point is within its direction if and only if the second point lies within the subspace.
explanatories.vsub_vadd_eq_vsub_sub: This theorem establishes that subtracting the sum of a group element and one point from another point is equivalent to first subtracting the point from the other and then subtracting the group element.
explanatories.add_comm: This theorem asserts that the addition operation in a commutative magma is commutative, meaning the sum of two elements does not depend on the order in which they are added.
explanatories.Submodule.add_mem: This theorem asserts that the sum of two elements from a submodule of a module is also an element of that submodule.
explanatories.Submodule.mem_orthogonal': A vector is in the orthogonal complement of a subspace if and only if it is orthogonal to every vector in that subspace when the inner product is taken in the reverse order.
explanatories.neg_sub: The negation of the difference between two elements in a subtraction monoid is equal to the difference of the second element from the first.
explanatories.inner_neg_left: This theorem asserts that negating the first argument of the inner product results in the negation of the inner product value, demonstrating the property of linearly reflecting the vector in the inner product space.
explanatories.orthogonalProjection_inner_eq_zero: The inner product of the difference between a point and its orthogonal projection onto a subspace with any vector in that subspace is zero.
explanatories.neg_zero: This theorem states that in a type with a negation operation and zero element, the negation of zero is equal to zero.
explanatories.Set.mem_inter: If an element belongs to two sets, it also belongs to their intersection.
explanatories.Set.mem_singleton_iff: An element belongs to a singleton set if and only if it is equal to the unique element in that set.
explanatories.AffineMap.linear: This defines a method to extract the linear part of an affine map between two affine spaces, resulting in a linear transformation between their corresponding vector spaces.
explanatories.And.intro: This states that if two propositions are true, then their conjunction is also true.
explanatories.AffineIsometryEquiv.mk': The definition establishes a method to create an affine isometry equivalence between two affine spaces by relating a mapping and its linear isometric counterpart at a specific reference point.
explanatories.AffineIsometryEquiv.symm: The definition specifies a method to obtain the inverse affine isometry equivalence between two affine spaces given an affine isometry equivalence.

  P ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] P
EuclideanGeometry.reflection.comment:
Reflection in an affine subspace, which is expected to be nonempty
and complete. The word "reflection" is sometimes understood to mean
specifically reflection in a codimension-one subspace, and sometimes
more generally to cover operations such as reflection in a point. The
definition here, of reflection in an affine subspace, is a more
general sense of the word that includes both those common cases.

explanatories.AffineSubspace.direction: This definition describes the direction of an affine subspace as the submodule formed by the differences of pairs of points within that subspace, with the exception of the zero submodule for an empty affine subspace.
explanatories.Eq.symm: Equality is symmetric, meaning that if one element is equal to another, then the second is equal to the first.
explanatories.Ne.symm: If two elements are not equal to each other, then reversing their order also indicates that they are not equal.
explanatories.Exists.intro: If there is an element that satisfies a property, then it can be used to demonstrate the existence of at least one such element with that property.
explanatories.AffineSubspace.mk': This definition constructs an affine subspace from a specified point and its associated direction.
explanatories.orthogonalProjection: The orthogonal projection is a linear map that takes a point from an inner product space to its closest point in a complete subspace.
explanatories.vsub_vadd_eq_vsub_sub: This theorem establishes that subtracting the sum of a group element and one point from another point is equivalent to first subtracting the point from the other and then subtracting the group element.
explanatories.EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjection: The orthogonal projection of a point onto a nonempty affine subspace is defined as a linear map that captures the point's closest approach to that subspace.
explanatories.EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjection_l: The orthogonal projection operation on an affine subspace corresponds to a linear map that projects points onto that subspace in the direction defined by its associated submodule.
explanatories.And.intro: This states that if two propositions are true, then their conjunction is also true.
explanatories.EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjection_m: The orthogonal projection of a point that lies within a nonempty affine subspace is equal to the point itself.
explanatories.AffineIsometryEquiv.mk': The definition establishes a method to create an affine isometry equivalence between two affine spaces by relating a mapping and its linear isometric counterpart at a specific reference point.
explanatories.Classical.arbitrary: A nonempty type can be represented by an arbitrary element chosen from it.
explanatories.AddAction.add_vadd: This theorem demonstrates that the vector addition operation is associative when combined with the addition operation of the underlying additive monoid.
explanatories.vsub_vadd: This theorem confirms that subtracting one element from another in an additive torsor and then adding the second element back results in the original first element.
explanatories.vadd_vsub: This theorem establishes that when an element from an additive group is added to a point in an additive torsor and then the same point is subtracted, the result is the original group element.
explanatories.reflection_apply: The reflection of a point in an inner product space across a submodule is given by twice the orthogonal projection of that point onto the submodule minus the original point.
explanatories.AffineMap.map_vadd: This theorem confirms that applying an affine map to the sum of a vector and a point yields a result equal to the sum of the image of the point under the affine map and the linear transformation of the vector.
explanatories.two_smul: This theorem demonstrates that multiplying an element of a module by two is equivalent to adding the element to itself.
explanatories.AffineIsometryEquiv.symm: The definition specifies a method to obtain the inverse affine isometry equivalence between two affine spaces given an affine isometry equivalence.

EuclideanGeometry.reflection.fullDefinition: def reflection (s : AffineSubspace ℝ P) [Nonempty s] [HasOrthogonalProjection s.direction] :     P ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] P :=   AffineIsometryEquiv.mk'     (fun p => ↑(orthogonalProjection s p) -ᵥ p +ᵥ (orthogonalProjection s p : P))     (_root_.reflection s.direction) (↑(Classical.arbitrary s))     (by       intro p       let v := p -ᵥ ↑(Classical.arbitrary s)       let a : V := _root_.orthogonalProjection s.direction v       let b : P := ↑(Classical.arbitrary s)       have key : a +ᵥ b -ᵥ (v +ᵥ b) +ᵥ (a +ᵥ b) = a + a - v +ᵥ (b -ᵥ b +ᵥ b) := by         rw [← add_vadd, vsub_vadd_eq_vsub_sub, vsub_vadd, vadd_vsub]         congr 1         abel       dsimp only       rwa [reflection_apply, (vsub_vadd p b).symm, AffineMap.map_vadd, orthogonalProjection_linear,         vadd_vsub, orthogonalProjection_mem_subspace_eq_self, two_smul])
EuclideanGeometry.reflection.description: Reflection in an affine subspace is defined as an affine isometry that describes how points are symmetrically mapped across that subspace.

EuclideanGeometry.inner_vsub_vsub_of_mem.comment:
Suppose that `p₁` and `p₂` lie in spheres `s₁` and `s₂`. Then the vector between the centers
of those spheres is orthogonal to that between `p₁` and `p₂`; this is a version of
`inner_vsub_vsub_of_dist_eq_of_dist_eq` for bundled spheres. (In two dimensions, this says that
the diagonals of a kite are orthogonal.)

EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.secondInter.comment:
The second intersection of a sphere with a line through a point on that sphere; that point
if it is the only point of intersection of the line with the sphere. The intended use of this
definition is when `p ∈ s`; the definition does not use `s.radius`, so in general it returns
the second intersection with the sphere through `p` and with center `s.center`.

EuclideanGeometry.Sphere.secondInter.description: The definition describes the calculation of the second intersection point of a sphere with a line that passes through a point on the sphere, under the assumption that this point is the only intersection of the line with the sphere.

  [HasOrthogonalProjection s.direction] {ps : Set P} (hnps : ps.Nonempty) {p : P} (hps : ps ⊆ ↑s) (hp : p ∉ s)
  (hu : ∃! cs, cs.center ∈ s ∧ ps ⊆ Metric.sphere cs.center cs.radius) :

EuclideanGeometry.existsUnique_dist_eq_o.comment:
The induction step for the existence and uniqueness of the
circumcenter.  Given a nonempty set of points in a nonempty affine
subspace whose direction is complete, such that there is a unique
(circumcenter, circumradius) pair for those points in that subspace,
and a point `p` not in that subspace, there is a unique (circumcenter,
circumradius) pair for the set with `p` added, in the span of the
subspace with `p` added.

Affine.Simplex.mongePoint.code:
Affine.Simplex.mongePoint.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V]
  [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] {n : ℕ} (s : Simplex ℝ P n) : P
Affine.Simplex.mongePoint.comment:
The Monge point of a simplex (in 2 or more dimensions) is a
generalization of the orthocenter of a triangle.  It is defined to be
the intersection of the Monge planes, where a Monge plane is the
(n-1)-dimensional affine subspace of the subspace spanned by the
simplex that passes through the centroid of an (n-2)-dimensional face
and is orthogonal to the opposite edge (in 2 dimensions, this is the
same as an altitude).  The circumcenter O, centroid G and Monge point
M are collinear in that order on the Euler line, with OG : GM = (n-1): 2.
Here, we use that ratio to define the Monge point (so resulting
in a point that equals the centroid in 0 or 1 dimensions), and then
show in subsequent lemmas that the point so defined lies in the Monge
planes and is their unique point of intersection.

explanatories.Finset.centroid: This definition identifies the centroid as a point associated with a finite set of points, specifically meant for situations where the number of points is non-zero after conversion to a different type.
explanatories.Affine.Simplex.points: The points of a simplex in an affine space can be indexed by a finite natural number, mapping each index to a corresponding point.
explanatories.Affine.Simplex.circumcenter: This definition describes the circumcenter of a simplex as a specific point within the associated space that serves as the center of the circle passing through all the vertices of the simplex.

Affine.Simplex.mongePoint.fullDefinition: def mongePoint {n : ℕ} (s : Simplex ℝ P n) : P :=   (((n + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) / ((n - 1 : ℕ) : ℝ)) •       ((univ : Finset (Fin (n + 1))).centroid ℝ s.points -ᵥ s.circumcenter) +ᵥ     s.circumcenter
Affine.Simplex.mongePoint.description: The Monge point of a simplex is defined as the intersection of the Monge planes, generalizing the concept of the orthocenter in triangles and relating the circumcenter, centroid, and Monge point collinearly on the Euler line.

EuclideanGeometry.exists_of_range_subset.code:
EuclideanGeometry.exists_of_range_subset_orthocentricSystem.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2}
  [NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] {t : Triangle ℝ P}
  (ho : t.orthocenter ∉ Set.range t.points) {p : Fin 3 → P}
  (hps : Set.range p ⊆ insert t.orthocenter (Set.range t.points)) (hpi : Function.Injective p) :
  (∃ i₁ i₂ i₃ j₂ j₃,
      i₁ ≠ i₂ ∧
        i₁ ≠ i₃ ∧
          i₂ ≠ i₃ ∧
            (∀ (i : Fin 3), i = i₁ ∨ i = i₂ ∨ i = i₃) ∧
              p i₁ = t.orthocenter ∧ j₂ ≠ j₃ ∧ t.points j₂ = p i₂ ∧ t.points j₃ = p i₃) ∨
    Set.range p = Set.range t.points
EuclideanGeometry.exists_of_range_subset.comment:
This is an auxiliary lemma giving information about the relation
of two triangles in an orthocentric system; it abstracts some
reasoning, with no geometric content, that is common to some other
lemmas.  Suppose the orthocentric system is generated by triangle `t`,
and we are given three points `p` in the orthocentric system.  Then
either we can find indices `i₁`, `i₂` and `i₃` for `p` such that `p
i₁` is the orthocenter of `t` and `p i₂` and `p i₃` are points `j₂`
and `j₃` of `t`, or `p` has the same points as `t`.

euclidean_geometry.exists_of_range_subse.code:
EuclideanGeometry.exists_of_range_subset_orthocentricSystem.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2}
  [NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] {t : Triangle ℝ P}
  (ho : t.orthocenter ∉ Set.range t.points) {p : Fin 3 → P}
  (hps : Set.range p ⊆ insert t.orthocenter (Set.range t.points)) (hpi : Function.Injective p) :
  (∃ i₁ i₂ i₃ j₂ j₃,
      i₁ ≠ i₂ ∧
        i₁ ≠ i₃ ∧
          i₂ ≠ i₃ ∧
            (∀ (i : Fin 3), i = i₁ ∨ i = i₂ ∨ i = i₃) ∧
              p i₁ = t.orthocenter ∧ j₂ ≠ j₃ ∧ t.points j₂ = p i₂ ∧ t.points j₃ = p i₃) ∨
    Set.range p = Set.range t.points
euclidean_geometry.exists_of_range_subse.comment:
This is an auxiliary lemma giving information about the relation
of two triangles in an orthocentric system; it abstracts some
reasoning, with no geometric content, that is common to some other
lemmas.  Suppose the orthocentric system is generated by triangle `t`,
and we are given three points `p` in the orthocentric system.  Then
either we can find indices `i₁`, `i₂` and `i₃` for `p` such that `p
i₁` is the orthocenter of `t` and `p i₂` and `p i₃` are points `j₂`
and `j₃` of `t`, or `p` has the same points as `t`.
